# Craft for five web genres

For article, casestudy, column and opinion, work as a skilled Swedish journalist at the professional level of SvD, DN, DI, Fokus, Ny Teknik, Filter or Forskning & Framsteg. For webcopy, work as an experienced Swedish copywriter and UX writer trusted by leading agencies and brands. These are standards of craft, not voices to imitate.

In every target language, keep that Swedish editorial or communicative tradition in the angle, disposition, storytelling, address and tone. Think and write wholly in the target language: its Language Resource governs vocabulary, idiom, syntax, punctuation and typography. A native professional should hear a colleague, not a translation. Language choice changes the language surface, not the chosen craft.

## Web reading

Give the reader a clear angle or task and useful ways into the text. Let facts and reasoning carry explanation; choose any narrative devices for what they contribute. Headings orient according to the genre, paragraphs hold connected thoughts, and varied rhythm supports both scanning and sustained reading.

For article, casestudy, column and opinion, the [article anatomy](article-anatomy.md) fixes the parts, their order and their dimensions.
# Article anatomy

The fixed skeleton of a text in the genres `article`, `casestudy`, `column` and `opinion`; *article* below means a text in any of them. The anatomy fixes which parts the text has, their order and their dimensions. Angle, argument, voice and language are outside it.

A statement below has one of three strengths:

- A plain statement is a requirement: it holds in every conforming text.
- *Should* marks a norm: follow it as a requirement, and depart only when following it is impossible or the departure is clearly better for the reader.
- *Most* states what is typical across the whole text; each single paragraph or section follows its own content.

A text conforms when every part is present in the order shown and all three hold. Limits are exact; verify each one by counting.

A review of a finished text reports a part the text lacks as missing rather than writing it, and repairs only the parts the text has.

## Order

```text
Headline
Standfirst
Byline
Lead
Subheading        ┐ a section; one or more
Paragraphs        ┘
Last subheading   ┐ the ending
Paragraphs        ┘
```

Each part appears once, except the section, which repeats. The first subheading follows the lead directly. The body is everything from the lead through the ending.

The headline is the text's level-1 heading (HTML `h1`, Markdown `#`), and every subheading is a level-2 heading (HTML `h2`, Markdown `##`). The text should use these two levels only. Where an academic text would nest a level-3 heading, a further level-2 subheading usually serves; a level-3 heading is for the rare text whose structure truly demands one.

## Headline

- 20–70 characters, spaces included.
- It should be three to eight words and at most 60 characters.
- It is written as [Headlines](headlines.md) says.

## Standfirst

The standfirst is a summarising paragraph that introduces the article and stands on its own. It is a full paragraph; a deck — a subtitle or one-line teaser — is a different device and no substitute for it.

- One paragraph, at most 60 words.
- Self-contained: a reader who sees only the standfirst understands it fully.
- It says what the article is about and what the reader gains from reading it.
- It entices the reader to read on.

## Byline

One line naming the author. In English: `By <author>`. In another language, that language's conventional byline form. The author is the one the brief names; when it names none, the author is the user.

## Lead

The lead is the first paragraph of the body: one paragraph, meeting every requirement under *Paragraphs*. It introduces the subject and gives the reader a clear expectation of what they will learn by reading on.

### Standfirst and lead

Both open the text. Each works without the other, and read together they never repeat:

- The body reads complete without the standfirst, which is often shown apart from the body or skipped. The lead introduces every person, thing and event it mentions, and nothing in the body points back to the standfirst.
- They should begin with different first words, and an everyday word such as *the* or *it* counts like any other.
- Read in sequence, the lead advances. A reader who has just read the standfirst meets the lead as new material, never as the standfirst said again; what the body needs from the standfirst is named again in passing, and the lead moves on.

## Paragraphs

- Each paragraph holds one thought, and the thought sets its length. Most paragraphs come to two or three sentences. A thought that takes one sentence, or four or five, gets exactly that.
- A break may also fall for drama: a single sentence, or a single word, stands alone when isolating it creates an effect the text needs.
- Sentence length varies within the paragraph, giving the text a natural rhythm.
- A paragraph should be at most 80 words, so that a web reader takes it in at a glance. Eighty is the outer edge; aim well below it.

## Subheadings and sections

A section is a subheading plus the paragraphs under it.

- A subheading is at most 70 characters, spaces included.
- It describes clearly what the paragraphs under it are about, and it is written as [Headlines](headlines.md) says.
- A section holds at least one paragraph and should hold at most three. Most sections hold two or three.

## Ending

The ending is a section of its own, opened by its own subheading, after at least one other section. It is the last section, and it is short: one paragraph can be enough. It does two things:

- It shows that the expectation the lead set has been met.
- It calls the reader to action, and the action follows from the article's content. The selected genre says what that action is in its kind of text.

The last section is the ending when its subheading and paragraphs close the piece — the call to action, the reflection, the recommendation or the next step — and it opens no new line of argument. Stating the recommendation or proposal the text has built towards is closing content, even where the last section is the first place the text states it in full; so are the writer's own reservation about it and the call to try or adopt it. What makes a section carry the argument is reasons or evidence the conclusion rests on that no earlier section gave. A last section that states the proposal, admits a doubt about it and asks the reader to act on it brings none, and is the ending. A section that carries the argument with a closing line appended is not an ending.
# Headlines

How a headline is written, in any genre that links this file. A headline lets the reader judge at once whether the text is for them: it states the core of the text as briefly and precisely as it can, and it is understood on its own, with no image, standfirst or surrounding page to explain it. *Headline* here covers a text's subheadings too; for a subheading, the text is its section.

## Statement or label

A text that reports, explains, argues, decides or narrates gets a statement headline: a clause that says what the text says. A text the reader looks things up in or navigates by — a policy, a manual, opening hours, a contact page — gets a plain label naming what it holds: *Privacy policy*, where a statement would read *How we protect your data*. Everything below is about the statement headline.

## What a statement headline does

- It states the angle: the single most important message, the sentence that would remain if only one could. A subject alone is a label. Test: the headline could not head a different text on the same subject.
- It is a simple clause — subject, active verb, object where there is one — in straight word order, and in the present tense where that fits: *Council introduces free bus travel*.
- The most important keyword comes first.
- A concrete detail stands in it when the detail carries the message: a number, a date, a place. *Three schools to close this autumn* beats *Changes to school organisation*.
- The reader sees what they gain: a decision, a fact, a change. An instructional text may address the reader directly (*you*, *your*) and open on *How to*, *Why* or *Here's*.
- It is as short as the angle allows. Modifiers, repetition and filler go; a keyword that carries meaning stays. The format the text follows sets the limits.
- It sounds like something a person would say aloud.
- Its words are ones this audience knows. A technical term is the right keyword for specialists and noise for a general reader, and the same holds for names and abbreviations.
- Its tone is the text's tone, and never louder. Illness, accidents, crime and crises get a sober, understated headline; a light text can carry more personality.
- It is plain before it is clever. It works in full for a reader who misses every allusion, so a pun or a reference never carries the meaning.
- It gives the answer. Journalists hold a question headline to be the wrong form, and so does this: it is a deliberate exception, natural over a text built as questions and answers, and available where the text truly leaves the question open and the headline is meant to assert nothing.
- The verb does the work. A colon standing in for a verb, a clipped quotation and headline-speak all give way to the full clause.
- It complements what follows. Headline and standfirst, or subheading and the first sentence under it, say different things in different words.

## Every word supported

A headline claims only what its text claims. Every figure, name, claim and conclusion in it is in the text, at the text's own strength: never sharper, never more general, never a conclusion the text does not draw. A reader who finishes the text finds that the headline told the truth about it.

## A subheading over a quotation

A quotation in a section is there to carry what only its speaker can say: a judgement, a figure, a concession. A subheading standing over it, however far down the section the quotation stands, leaves that to the quotation. It states the section's angle from what the rest of the section says, or, where the quotation is the section's point, names the subject, the occasion or the speaker the quotation speaks to, and not the point itself. Test: a reader who has just read the subheading meets the quotation as new material, never as the subheading said again. *The clinic would double its training time*, over a head nurse saying *Next time I would double the training time before we switch*, has spent the quotation before the reader reaches it; *The head nurse looks back on the switch* leaves it to her.

The quotation bridge is the narrative sentence or clause that stands immediately before a quotation and leads the reader into it, including a speech tag that carries anything besides the attribution. The genre that quotes says what a quotation bridge may carry. A subheading standing over a quotation is outside the quotation bridge and is governed by this section.

## Getting there

Settle the reader and the angle before wording anything. Then write three to five variants and keep the clearest, which is rarely the cleverest. Word a subheading from its whole section, once the section is written, in words its first sentence does not use, and leave a quotation standing under it the judgement, figure or concession it is there to carry.

### SS-1. Singular officer provenance is not supplied

**Draft passage:** “The officer’s report for Lervik’s municipal executive board meeting on 18 June”

**Missing or changed support:** The source identifies the type and occasion of the administrative document. It supplies no singular officer, document owner or author count. The draft’s singular possessive adds that provenance.

**Concrete two-direction test:**
1. A municipal department could issue this tjänsteutlåtande jointly through several officials, with no single officer owning or authoring it. The supplied material permits this: it names the document and the administration but contains no statement excluding joint institutional authorship. The Swedish statement still holds; the singular “the officer’s report” does not have the provenance it names.
2. Conversely, a single officer could produce a report for that meeting that is a supporting briefing rather than the formal tjänsteutlåtande. The draft’s generic document description could hold while the source’s specific administrative-document designation does not. The supplied material contains no statement equating every officer report with the tjänsteutlåtande.

This is a source-support issue in translated descriptive prose, not a quotation-translation issue.

**Concrete two-direction test:**
1. A nationwide association could use one of the municipality’s association premises. “Föreningslokaler” remains true, while classifying those premises as being for “local associations” adds a restriction that need not hold. Nothing supplied excludes national associations or their bookings.
2. If a venue is for local associations, it is also a venue for associations; there is no reverse counterexample on that restriction. The asymmetry confirms that the draft narrows the source term rather than reproducing its scope.

**Smallest supported repair:** Delete “local”, producing “all seven venues for associations”.

This is a source-support issue in translated descriptive prose, not a quotation-translation issue.

No unsupported legal duty, protest, discrimination event, party motive, savings amount, causal saving effect, telephone-user motive or personal experience appears. Reported figures are attributed where they support the argument. Cost uncertainty and the board’s three possible final decisions remain explicit. Editorial judgments about the comparison and the trial belong to the commissioned author and are defensible as written.

## Source-support findings and minimum repairs

### SS-1. Singular officer provenance is not supplied

**Draft passage:** “The officer’s report for Lervik’s municipal executive board meeting on 18 June”

**Exact support:** “Tjänsteutlåtandet inför kommunstyrelsens möte den 18 juni”

**Missing or changed support:** The source identifies the type and occasion of the administrative document. It supplies no singular officer, document owner or author count. The draft’s singular possessive adds that provenance.

**Concrete two-direction test:**
1. A municipal department could issue this tjänsteutlåtande jointly through several officials, with no single officer owning or authoring it. The supplied material permits this: it names the document and the administration but contains no statement excluding joint institutional authorship. The Swedish statement still holds; the singular “the officer’s report” does not have the provenance it names.
2. Conversely, a single officer could produce a report for that meeting that is a supporting briefing rather than the formal tjänsteutlåtande. The draft’s generic document description could hold while the source’s specific administrative-document designation does not. The supplied material contains no statement equating every officer report with the tjänsteutlåtande.

**Smallest supported repair:** Replace “The officer’s report” with “The administrative report”. Keep the meeting, proposal, dates and all substantive claims.

This is a source-support issue in translated descriptive prose, not a quotation-translation issue.

### SS-2. “Local” restricts the associations beyond the source

**Draft passage:** “all seven venues for local associations”

**Exact support:** “alla sju lokaler”; their service is identified as “bokning av föreningslokaler”.

**Missing or changed support:** “Föreningslokaler” supplies premises for associations. It does not say those associations must be locally based. The brief’s local audience and fictional municipal setting do not establish the associations’ geographical scope.

**Concrete two-direction test:**
1. A nationwide association could use one of the municipality’s association premises. “Föreningslokaler” remains true, while classifying those premises as being for “local associations” adds a restriction that need not hold. Nothing supplied excludes national associations or their bookings.
2. If a venue is for local associations, it is also a venue for associations; there is no reverse counterexample on that restriction. The asymmetry confirms that the draft narrows the source term rather than reproducing its scope.

**Smallest supported repair:** Delete “local”, producing “all seven venues for associations”.

This is a source-support issue in translated descriptive prose, not a quotation-translation issue.

## Material examined and scope

Read the complete supplied source, `source.md`, and the complete current draft, `draft.md`, including the headline, standfirst, byline and four subheadings. The source is Swedish; the draft is British English. The source identifies this as a fictional Lervik policy debate. There is no additional factual material and no direct speech quotation in the draft.

The comparison below distinguishes the author’s supported standpoint and reasoning from factual assertions. It does not require external evidence for an argument that the brief commissions Sanna Ek to make. It does require support for the factual premises of that argument, including the referents and restrictions introduced by translated terms.

## Complete claim accounting

### 1. Headline: requested action and timing

**Draft:** “Lervik should test before ending telephone bookings”

**Source:** “Tes: kommunstyrelsen bör skjuta upp ett permanent byte till enbart digital bokning av föreningslokaler och först pröva ett halvår med både telefon och webb.”

**Comparison:** This is the commissioned recommendation, expressed as a headline. “Lervik” functions as the municipality whose executive board makes the decision; it does not assert an additional actor or a separate decision. “Before” preserves the order of trial first, permanent change later. The title does not assert that telephone booking has already ended. Its omitted trial length and permanent-change qualification are supplied in the article. Supported as the author’s advocacy.

### 2. Standfirst: what booking totals establish

**Draft:** “Booking totals in Lervik’s pilot report do not measure residents’ ability to book online.”

**Source:** “Rapporten räknar bokningar, inte unika personer. Den mäter inte ålder, funktionsförmåga eller digital vana. Telefonbokningarna kan därför inte användas för att säga hur stor andel av invånarna som inte kan boka digitalt.”

**Comparison:** The subject of the draft’s negative is the booking totals, not every conceivable item of information in the report. The source expressly distinguishes bookings from people and denies that telephone totals establish the share of residents unable to book digitally. The draft’s ordinary contextual meaning is that booking totals are no measurement of residents’ digital-booking ability. It does not assert that all residents can book online, that no caller has difficulty, or that the report contains a measured population prevalence. Supported.

### 3. Standfirst: required comparison

**Draft:** “The municipal executive board must weigh staff costs against the value of telephone access”

**Source:** “Hon menar att kommunen först måste kunna väga arbetskostnaden mot värdet för användarna.”

**Contextual source:** “Att en bokning går via telefon är inte ett bevis för att någon inte kan använda webben. Det är ett skäl att ta reda på varför telefonen fortfarande används.”

**Comparison:** The source expressly attributes this position to Sanna. The byline and first-person body preserve her ownership of the argument; the standfirst reads as the article’s position, not as an independently established legal duty. “The municipal executive board” identifies the decision-making body named throughout the brief. “Staff costs” renders “arbetskostnaden”; “the value of telephone access” focuses the source’s value-to-users comparison on the route proposed for removal. That focus is the author’s supported argument about the proposal, rather than a claim that telephone access has a measured value. No legal requirement or quantified benefit is invented. Supported.

### 4. Standfirst: absent measurements and calculations

**Draft:** “yet the documents contain neither a time measurement nor a calculation of financial savings.”

**Source:** “Någon tidsmätning eller ekonomisk besparingsberäkning finns inte i handlingarna.”

**Comparison:** The subject, documentary scope and stated absences match. Financial savings is an idiomatic rendering of “ekonomisk besparingsberäkning” in this municipal staff-cost context. This says no calculation exists in the documents; it does not say savings cannot occur or have been disproved. Supported.

### 5. Byline: author and role

**Draft:** “By Sanna Ek, spokesperson for Öppna beslut”

**Source:** “Avsändare är Sanna Ek, talesperson för föreningen Öppna beslut.”

**Comparison:** The named author and spokesperson role match. The byline names the commissioned author, not the user. “Spokesperson” conveys no natural gender. The source later uses “Hon”, which conveys a female singular referent, but the draft adds no incompatible natural-gender assertion. Supported.

### 6. Opening: identity and date of the administrative document

**Draft:** “The officer’s report for Lervik’s municipal executive board meeting on 18 June”

**Source:** “Tjänsteutlåtandet inför kommunstyrelsens möte den 18 juni”

**Comparison:** The meeting, day and month match. No year has been added to the meeting date. “For” preserves the report’s relationship to the forthcoming meeting. “Municipal executive board” denotes “kommunstyrelsen” in this fictional municipality without importing UK council powers.

“The officer’s report” introduces a singular officer as the report’s source or owner where “Tjänsteutlåtandet” identifies an administrative document without supplying the number or identity of its responsible officials. This provenance difference is finding SS-1 below.

### 7. Opening: proposed removal, venues and start date

**Draft:** “proposes removing telephone booking from all seven venues for local associations from September.”

**Source:** “föreslår att telefonbokning tas bort för alla sju lokaler från september.”

**Earlier source defining the premises:** “Kommunens pilotrapport Bokning av föreningslokaler, 8 april 2026, gäller ett åtta veckor långt försök i två lokaler.”

**Brief defining the service:** “ett permanent byte till enbart digital bokning av föreningslokaler”

**Comparison:** Proposed status, telephone booking, all seven premises and September commencement match. The draft does not convert the proposal into an enacted decision. In this booking context “venues” identifies the premises, without asserting a particular building or room configuration. However, “local” modifies “associations” and adds a restriction absent from “föreningslokaler”. This is finding SS-2 below.

### 8. Opening: stance on digital booking

**Draft:** “I do not oppose digital booking.”

**Source:** “Hon motsätter sig inte digital bokning.”

**Comparison:** The first-person author is Sanna, established by the byline. The position matches. It does not assert support for every digital-only proposal. Supported.

### 9. Opening: representation and six-month request

**Draft:** “But on behalf of Öppna beslut, I urge the board to postpone a permanent switch and test telephone and web booking together for six months.”

**Source:** “Avsändare är Sanna Ek, talesperson för föreningen Öppna beslut. Tes: kommunstyrelsen bör skjuta upp ett permanent byte till enbart digital bokning av föreningslokaler och först pröva ett halvår med både telefon och webb.”

**Further source:** “Öppna beslut föreslår ett sex månader långt försök i alla sju lokaler, med båda bokningsvägarna kvar.”

**Comparison:** The spokesperson’s representative capacity, postponement, permanent switch, both routes and duration match. The preceding removal proposal settles the referent of “a permanent switch”; it is the proposed move to online-only booking. This is advocacy, not a report that a trial has been approved or funded. Supported.

### 10. First subheading: limits of booking information

**Draft:** “Bookings tell us too little about users”

**Source:** “Rapporten räknar bokningar, inte unika personer. Den mäter inte ålder, funktionsförmåga eller digital vana. Telefonbokningarna kan därför inte användas för att säga hur stor andel av invånarna som inte kan boka digitalt.”

**Comparison:** “Too little” evaluates the totals against the decision and investigation the brief says Sanna advocates. It is not a numerical assessment that 24 bookings is high or low. The immediately following paragraph specifies the information limits. Supported as the author’s argument.

### 11. Pilot identity, date, counts, duration and scope

**Draft:** “The municipality’s pilot report, dated 8 April 2026, records 96 web bookings and 24 telephone bookings during an eight-week trial at two venues.”

**Source:** “Kommunens pilotrapport Bokning av föreningslokaler, 8 april 2026, gäller ett åtta veckor långt försök i två lokaler. Under försöket gjordes 96 bokningar via webb och 24 via telefon.”

**Comparison:** Municipality ownership, date, eight-week duration, two-premises scope, booking unit, channels and numbers match. The draft attributes both counts directly to the pilot report where they carry the argument, as the boundaries require. It does not turn counts into unique users, people or population shares. The document title is omitted without substituting a different named document. Supported.

### 12. Unit counted

**Draft:** “Those are bookings, not unique people.”

**Source:** “Rapporten räknar bokningar, inte unika personer.”

**Comparison:** “Those” refers to the 96 and 24 immediately preceding bookings. Both count and exclusion match. This does not state how many unique people booked. Supported.

### 13. Variables not measured

**Draft:** “The report measures neither age nor functional ability nor familiarity with digital technology.”

**Source:** “Den mäter inte ålder, funktionsförmåga eller digital vana.”

**Comparison:** The subject and all three excluded measurements match. In this user-access context, “functional ability” names the personal capacity denoted by “funktionsförmåga”, and “familiarity with digital technology” naturally denotes the practical digital familiarity denoted by “digital vana”. No particular diagnosis, disability prevalence or technical competence score is supplied. The wording does not mean merely knowledge of technology as an academic subject. No concrete contextual mismatch warrants a finding.

### 14. Telephone count and population inference

**Draft:** “So the telephone figure cannot tell us what proportion of Lervik’s residents cannot book online.”

**Source:** “Telefonbokningarna kan därför inte användas för att säga hur stor andel av invånarna som inte kan boka digitalt.”

**Comparison:** The antecedent is the reported count of 24 telephone bookings. Scope, population, channel and inability claim match. “Cannot tell us” preserves the source’s exclusion of that inference; it does not convert unknown inability into known ability. Supported.

### 15. Telephone use does not prove inability

**Draft:** “Nor does choosing the telephone prove an inability to use the web.”

**Source:** “Sanna Eks ståndpunkt: ‘Att en bokning går via telefon är inte ett bevis för att någon inte kan använda webben.’”

**Comparison:** This is an indirect rendering of Sanna’s explicitly supplied standpoint. Choosing telephone booking is not asserted to have any particular motive, and the sentence does not deny that an individual might be unable to use the web. “Choosing” fits the source’s later “varför de väljer telefon eller webb”; it does not assert unrestricted choice or the absence of barriers. Supported.

### 16. Reason to investigate

**Draft:** “It gives us a reason to ask why that route is still used.”

**Source:** “Det är ett skäl att ta reda på varför telefonen fortfarande används.”

**Comparison:** “It” is telephone booking/use, and “that route” is telephone booking. Ongoing use and the author’s reason to investigate match. No reason for using it is invented. Supported.

### 17. Second subheading: comparison of staff time

**Draft:** “Staff time needs a fair comparison”

**Source:** “Under försöket ska förvaltningen registrera tidsåtgång per bokningsväg”

**Further source:** “Hon menar att kommunen först måste kunna väga arbetskostnaden mot värdet för användarna.”

**Comparison:** The proposed channel-specific timing and Sanna’s comparison underpin this evaluative subheading. “Fair” is her advocacy about how to assess the proposal, not an attributed finding that an existing measured comparison is unfair. Supported.

### 18. Administration’s objection and workflows

**Draft:** “The administration’s objection to keeping both routes is the administrative work across two channels: staff enter information in two workflows.”

**Source:** “Motivet i utlåtandet är att personalen ska slippa föra in uppgifter i två flöden. Någon tidsmätning eller ekonomisk besparingsberäkning finns inte i handlingarna. Förvaltningens verkliga invändning mot att behålla båda kanalerna är dubbel administration, inte att telefonanvändare är lata eller dyra.”

**Comparison:** The draft preserves the actual supplied objection and its stated operational basis. The source’s desire that staff be spared entering information in two workflows supports the work being avoided. It does not introduce an amount of time or money, laziness, expense per telephone user, party motives or a causal savings estimate. “Across two channels” is specified by the following clause; it does not reduce the objection to mere existence of two access routes. Supported.

### 19. Taking the concern seriously

**Draft:** “That concern deserves to be taken seriously.”

**Source:** “Förvaltningens verkliga invändning mot att behålla båda kanalerna är dubbel administration”

**Further source:** “Hon menar att kommunen först måste kunna väga arbetskostnaden mot värdet för användarna.”

**Comparison:** This is the author’s assessment of a supported objection. No outside party’s view is invented. It preserves the labour-cost side of the balance rather than changing the source’s factual motive. Supported argument.

### 20. Documentary absence, repeated in body

**Draft:** “But the documents provide no measurement of the time involved or calculation of financial savings.”

**Source:** “Någon tidsmätning eller ekonomisk besparingsberäkning finns inte i handlingarna.”

**Comparison:** The documentary scope and absent time/savings calculations match. The immediately preceding workflow detail settles “the time involved”. As in the standfirst, this is not a claim that nobody outside the documents has measured time or that savings are impossible. Supported.

### 21. Consequence for the board’s comparison

**Draft:** “Removing a route before establishing its value to users and the work it requires leaves the board without the comparison it needs.”

**Source:** “Hon menar att kommunen först måste kunna väga arbetskostnaden mot värdet för användarna.”

**Relevant factual source:** “Någon tidsmätning eller ekonomisk besparingsberäkning finns inte i handlingarna.”

**Proposed investigation:** “Under försöket ska förvaltningen registrera tidsåtgång per bokningsväg och be användarna frivilligt ange varför de väljer telefon eller webb.”

**Comparison:** This is Sanna’s argument for gathering the missing channel-specific evidence before a decision. It is conditional reasoning about removal before establishing the relevant comparison, not a report of an actual removal, a quantified causal effect, or an assertion that no information about users exists anywhere. “A route” is generic within the two-route proposal; “its” and “it” refer to that route. Supported argument.

### 22. Administrative simplicity and investigation

**Draft:** “Administrative simplicity is a reason to investigate the balance, not a substitute for doing so.”

**Source:** “Motivet i utlåtandet är att personalen ska slippa föra in uppgifter i två flöden.”

**Further source:** “Hon menar att kommunen först måste kunna väga arbetskostnaden mot värdet för användarna.”

**Comparison:** The first phrase characterises the supported aim of avoiding double administration. The rest is the author’s reasoning about what that aim justifies. No measured simplification, completed investigation or external consensus is claimed. Supported argument.

### 23. Third subheading: trial’s decision value

**Draft:** “A wider trial can inform the choice”

**Source:** “ett åtta veckor långt försök i två lokaler”

**Further source:** “Öppna beslut föreslår ett sex månader långt försök i alla sju lokaler, med båda bokningsvägarna kvar. Under försöket ska förvaltningen registrera tidsåtgång per bokningsväg och be användarna frivilligt ange varför de väljer telefon eller webb.”

**Following source:** “Därefter kan den avgöra om en kanal ska tas bort, ändras eller behållas.”

**Comparison:** “Wider” has an explicit comparison: seven premises rather than two, with a longer proposed period. “Can inform” is an argument about the purpose of collecting relevant evidence; it does not guarantee a particular result or savings. Supported.

### 24. Organisation’s proposal, duration and coverage

**Draft:** “Öppna beslut proposes keeping both booking routes for six months at all seven venues.”

**Source:** “Öppna beslut föreslår ett sex månader långt försök i alla sju lokaler, med båda bokningsvägarna kvar.”

**Comparison:** Proposer, proposed status, duration, both routes and all-seven coverage match. The previous subheading and following “During that trial” preserve the proposal’s trial status; this is not an indefinitely funded service promise. Supported.

### 25. Data gathering and voluntary reasons

**Draft:** “During that trial, the administration should record the time spent on each route and ask users to say voluntarily why they choose telephone or web booking.”

**Source:** “Under försöket ska förvaltningen registrera tidsåtgång per bokningsväg och be användarna frivilligt ange varför de väljer telefon eller webb.”

**Comparison:** The administration, proposed trial, per-route measurement, question, voluntary disclosure and two choices match. The draft’s “should” is a recommendation in the article and does not report an adopted administrative order. Voluntariness belongs to users giving reasons; the draft retains that scope. No age, disability or digital-literacy measurement is added. Supported.

### 26. Financing and costing: no claim

**Draft:** “We make no claim to have financed or costed that trial.”

**Source:** “Föreningen gör inget anspråk på att ha finansierat eller kostnadsberäknat försöket.”

**Comparison:** The preceding sentence identifies Öppna beslut, so “we” is the organisation speaking through its spokesperson. The draft retains the no-claim formulation. It does not replace it with an assertion that financing or costing definitely has not occurred. “Costed” is idiomatic British English for having calculated the trial’s costs. Supported.

### 27. Trial cost and board’s responsibility

**Draft:** “The executive board must consider its cost.”

**Source:** “Kostnaden behöver kommunstyrelsen ta ställning till.”

**Comparison:** The board and trial cost match. “Consider” alone is less explicit than taking a position, but the following sentence supplies the need to decide what the evidence-gathering is worth, and the final recommendation requires explicit cost consideration when agreeing the trial. Read in that context, the article does not claim a funded proposal or evade the board’s cost judgement. Supported; no factual certainty about the amount is introduced.

### 28. Evidence gathering also requires a decision

**Draft:** “Asking for better evidence does not remove the need to decide what gathering it is worth.”

**Source:** “Föreningen gör inget anspråk på att ha finansierat eller kostnadsberäknat försöket. Kostnaden behöver kommunstyrelsen ta ställning till.”

**Comparison:** This is the author’s reflection on the supported cost uncertainty and board responsibility. “It” refers to evidence, not an unidentified person. It adds no amount, available budget, financial calculation or claim of affordability. Supported argument.

### 29. Final subheading: evidence and decision

**Draft:** “Evidence should guide the final booking decision”

**Source:** “Tes: kommunstyrelsen bör skjuta upp ett permanent byte till enbart digital bokning av föreningslokaler och först pröva ett halvår med både telefon och webb.”

**Further source:** “Därefter kan den avgöra om en kanal ska tas bort, ändras eller behållas.”

**Comparison:** This is the commissioned evidence-first position. “Final” distinguishes the permanent channel decision from the preliminary trial; it does not claim the future decision is legally irrevocable. Supported advocacy.

### 30. Final paragraph: immediate board recommendation and cost uncertainty

**Draft:** “Lervik’s municipal executive board should now postpone the permanent switch and agree a six-month trial of both routes, with its cost explicitly considered.”

**Source:** “Tes: kommunstyrelsen bör skjuta upp ett permanent byte till enbart digital bokning av föreningslokaler och först pröva ett halvår med både telefon och webb.”

**Further source:** “Öppna beslut föreslår ett sex månader långt försök i alla sju lokaler, med båda bokningsvägarna kvar.”

**Cost qualification:** “Föreningen gör inget anspråk på att ha finansierat eller kostnadsberäknat försöket. Kostnaden behöver kommunstyrelsen ta ställning till.”

**Comparison:** The named body, requested postponement, permanent-change referent, six-month trial and two routes match. “Now” is the timing of the author’s recommendation, not an invented event date. “Agree” is part of that recommendation, not a reported approval. “Its cost explicitly considered” keeps the trial’s cost before the board; together with the preceding no-costing/no-financing-claim sentence it preserves the supplied uncertainty. Supported.

### 31. Final paragraph: available decisions after the trial

**Draft:** “After that, it can decide whether to remove, change or retain a booking channel.”

**Source:** “Kostnaden behöver kommunstyrelsen ta ställning till. Därefter kan den avgöra om en kanal ska tas bort, ändras eller behållas.”

**Comparison:** “It” denotes the named municipal executive board. The decision’s timing follows the proposed trial and cost consideration, as in the source’s trial-and-decision sequence. The modality “can” and all three possible channel outcomes match. The draft does not prescribe retention as the only acceptable final decision. Supported.

## Pronoun accounting

Person, number and natural gender are accounted for independently of merely locating each referent.

- **“I”** in “I do not oppose” and “I urge”: first-person singular, no natural gender encoded. The source supplies Sanna as the author/spokesperson, gives her non-opposition, and commissions the recommendation. Swedish “Hon” is third-person singular and naturally female; changing to the authorised first-person authorial voice adds no gender claim.
- **“Those”** in “Those are bookings”: plural demonstrative, no natural gender, referring to the reported bookings. Source “bokningar” and the two counts establish plurality.
- **“us”** in “tell us too little”, “cannot tell us” and “gives us a reason”: first-person plural, no natural gender. These are inclusive author-and-reader positions in an opinion article for residents. They do not identify a measured group or assert that every resident holds Sanna’s opinion. The factual inference limits remain those supplied.
- **“It”** in “It gives us a reason”: third-person singular, no natural gender, referring to the fact of telephone booking/use. Swedish “Det” similarly denotes that fact. Neither identifies a human whose gender would need support.
- **“that route”**, **“both routes”**, **“each route”** and **“both booking routes”** refer to telephone and web booking. The source expressly supplies both channels and their uses. Singular “that route” is telephone; “each” distributes the proposed timing measurement over the two.
- **“That concern”** denotes double administration. Demonstrative singular, no natural gender; the source expressly supplies the objection.
- **“its”** in “its value to users” and **“it”** in “the work it requires”: third-person singular, no natural gender, referring to the hypothetical booking route. The source supplies routes and the cost/value comparison. The possessives do not assert a measured value or duration.
- **“it”** in “the comparison it needs”: third-person singular, no natural gender, referring to the board. The source assigns the decision and needed comparison to the municipality/board. It does not assert that the board has publicly adopted Sanna’s view.
- **“doing so”** refers to investigating the balance. It supplies no person, number or gender assertion.
- **“they”** in “why they choose”: third-person plural, natural gender unspecified, referring to users. Source “användarna” and “de väljer” establish plural users; no female or male user population is asserted.
- **“We”** in “We make no claim”: first-person plural, natural gender unspecified, the organisation’s institutional voice through its named spokesperson. The source’s singular “Föreningen” establishes who stands behind the statement; “we” does not assert a specific number of authors, staff or funded participants.
- **“its”** in “consider its cost” and “with its cost explicitly considered”: third-person singular, no natural gender, referring to the trial. Source “Kostnaden” in the trial paragraph settles that relationship.
- **“it”** in “gathering it”: third-person singular, no natural gender, referring to evidence. This is the author’s reasoning about the proposed data gathering.
- **“that”** in “After that”: a singular demonstrative reference to the proposed trial and consideration sequence, with no natural gender.
- **“it”** in “it can decide”: third-person singular, no natural gender, the board. Source “den” refers to “kommunstyrelsen”; Swedish common grammatical gender is not a separate natural-gender assertion about a human.

The draft’s nonpersonal English “it/its” references do not carry the source’s purely grammatical Swedish gender into human natural-gender claims. No masculine or female user group, unnamed individual user, first-hand personal experience or additional speaker has been invented.

## Source-support findings and minimum repairs

### SS-1. Singular officer provenance is not supplied

**Draft passage:** “The officer’s report for Lervik’s municipal executive board meeting on 18 June”

**Exact support:** “Tjänsteutlåtandet inför kommunstyrelsens möte den 18 juni”

**Missing or changed support:** The source identifies the type and occasion of the administrative document. It supplies no singular officer, document owner or author count. The draft’s singular possessive adds that provenance.

**Concrete two-direction test:**
1. A municipal department could issue this tjänsteutlåtande jointly through several officials, with no single officer owning or authoring it. The supplied material permits this: it names the document and the administration but contains no statement excluding joint institutional authorship. The Swedish statement still holds; the singular “the officer’s report” does not have the provenance it names.
2. Conversely, a single officer could produce a report for that meeting that is a supporting briefing rather than the formal tjänsteutlåtande. The draft’s generic document description could hold while the source’s specific administrative-document designation does not. The supplied material contains no statement equating every officer report with the tjänsteutlåtande.

**Smallest supported repair:** Replace “The officer’s report” with “The administrative report”. Keep the meeting, proposal, dates and all substantive claims.

This is a source-support issue in translated descriptive prose, not a quotation-translation issue.

### SS-2. “Local” restricts the associations beyond the source

**Draft passage:** “all seven venues for local associations”

**Exact support:** “alla sju lokaler”; their service is identified as “bokning av föreningslokaler”.

**Missing or changed support:** “Föreningslokaler” supplies premises for associations. It does not say those associations must be locally based. The brief’s local audience and fictional municipal setting do not establish the associations’ geographical scope.

**Concrete two-direction test:**
1. A nationwide association could use one of the municipality’s association premises. “Föreningslokaler” remains true, while classifying those premises as being for “local associations” adds a restriction that need not hold. Nothing supplied excludes national associations or their bookings.

Read the complete supplied source, source.md, and the complete current draft, draft.md, including the headline, standfirst, byline and four subheadings. The source is Swedish; the draft is British English. The source identifies this as a fictional Lervik policy debate. It does not require external evidence for an argument that the brief commissions Sanna Ek to make. It does require support for the factual premises of that argument, including the referents and restrictions introduced by translated terms.

## Complete claim accounting

### 1. Headline: requested action and timing

**Draft:** “Lervik should test before ending telephone bookings”

**Source:** “Tes: kommunstyrelsen bör skjuta upp ett permanent byte till enbart digital bokning av föreningslokaler och först pröva ett halvår med både telefon och webb.”

**Comparison:** This is the commissioned recommendation, expressed as a headline. “Lervik” functions as the municipality whose executive board makes the decision; it does not assert an additional actor or a separate decision. “Before” preserves the order of trial first, permanent change later. The title does not assert that telephone booking has already ended. Its omitted trial length and permanent-change qualification are supplied in the article. Supported as the author’s advocacy.

### 2. Standfirst: what booking totals establish

**Draft:** “Booking totals in Lervik’s pilot report do not measure residents’ ability to book online.”

**Source:** “Rapporten räknar bokningar, inte unika personer. Den mäter inte ålder, funktionsförmåga eller digital vana. Telefonbokningarna kan därför inte användas för att säga hur stor andel av invånarna som inte kan boka digitalt.”

**Comparison:** The subject of the draft’s negative is the booking totals, not every conceivable item of information in the report. The source expressly distinguishes bookings from people and denies that telephone totals establish the share of residents unable to book digitally. The draft’s ordinary contextual meaning is that booking totals are no measurement of residents’ digital-booking ability. It does not assert that all residents can book online, that no caller has difficulty, or that the report contains a measured population prevalence. Supported.

### 3. Standfirst: required comparison

**Draft:** “The municipal executive board must weigh staff costs against the value of telephone access”

**Source:** “Hon menar att kommunen först måste kunna väga arbetskostnaden mot värdet för användarna.”

**Contextual source:** “Att en bokning går via telefon är inte ett bevis för att någon inte kan använda webben. Det är ett skäl att ta reda på varför telefonen fortfarande används.”

**Comparison:** The source expressly attributes this position to Sanna. The byline and first-person body preserve her ownership of the argument; the standfirst reads as the article’s position, not as an independently established legal duty. “The municipal executive board” identifies the decision-making body named throughout the brief. “Staff costs” renders “arbetskostnaden”; “the value of telephone access” focuses the source’s value-to-users comparison on the route proposed for removal. That focus is the author’s supported argument about the proposal, rather than a claim that telephone access has a measured value. No legal requirement or quantified benefit is invented. Supported.

### 4. Standfirst: absent measurements and calculations

**Draft:** “yet the documents contain neither a time measurement nor a calculation of financial savings.”

**Source:** “Någon tidsmätning eller ekonomisk besparingsberäkning finns inte i handlingarna.”

**Comparison:** The subject, documentary scope and stated absences match. Financial savings is an idiomatic rendering of “ekonomisk besparingsberäkning” in this municipal staff-cost context. This says no calculation exists in the documents; it does not say savings cannot occur or have been disproved. Supported.

### 5. Byline: author and role

**Draft:** “By Sanna Ek, spokesperson for Öppna beslut”

**Source:** “Avsändare är Sanna Ek, talesperson för föreningen Öppna beslut.”

**Comparison:** The named author and spokesperson role match. The byline names the commissioned author, not the user. “Spokesperson” conveys no natural gender. The source later uses “Hon”, which conveys a female singular referent, but the draft adds no incompatible natural-gender assertion. Supported.

### 6. Opening: identity and date of the administrative document

**Draft:** “The officer’s report for Lervik’s municipal executive board meeting on 18 June”

**Source:** “Tjänsteutlåtandet inför kommunstyrelsens möte den 18 juni”

**Comparison:** The meeting, day and month match. No year has been added to the meeting date. “For” preserves the report’s relationship to the forthcoming meeting. “Municipal executive board” denotes “kommunstyrelsen” in this fictional municipality without importing UK council powers.

“The officer’s report” introduces a singular officer as the report’s source or owner where “Tjänsteutlåtandet” identifies an administrative document without supplying the number or identity of its responsible officials. This provenance difference is finding SS-1 below.

### 7. Opening: proposed removal, venues and start date

**Draft:** “proposes removing telephone booking from all seven venues for local associations from September.”

**Source:** “föreslår att telefonbokning tas bort för alla sju lokaler från september.”

**Earlier source defining the premises:** “Kommunens pilotrapport Bokning av föreningslokaler, 8 april 2026, gäller ett åtta veckor långt försök i två lokaler.”

**Brief defining the service:** “ett permanent byte till enbart digital bokning av föreningslokaler”

**Comparison:** Proposed status, telephone booking, all seven premises and September commencement match. The draft does not convert the proposal into an enacted decision. In this booking context “venues” identifies the premises, without asserting a particular building or room configuration. However, “local” modifies “associations” and adds a restriction absent from “föreningslokaler”. This is finding SS-2 below.

### 8. Opening: stance on digital booking

**Draft:** “I do not oppose digital booking.”

**Source:** “Hon motsätter sig inte digital bokning.”

**Comparison:** The first-person author is Sanna, established by the byline. The position matches. It does not assert support for every digital-only proposal. Supported.

### 9. Opening: representation and six-month request

**Draft:** “But on behalf of Öppna beslut, I urge the board to postpone a permanent switch and test telephone and web booking together for six months.”

**Source:** “Avsändare är Sanna Ek, talesperson för föreningen Öppna beslut. Tes: kommunstyrelsen bör skjuta upp ett permanent byte till enbart digital bokning av föreningslokaler och först pröva ett halvår med både telefon och webb.”

**Further source:** “Öppna beslut föreslår ett sex månader långt försök i alla sju lokaler, med båda bokningsvägarna kvar.”

**Comparison:** The spokesperson’s representative capacity, postponement, permanent switch, both routes and duration match. The preceding removal proposal settles the referent of “a permanent switch”; it is the proposed move to online-only booking. This is advocacy, not a report that a trial has been approved or funded. Supported.

### 10. First subheading: limits of booking information

**Draft:** “Bookings tell us too little about users”

**Source:** “Rapporten räknar bokningar, inte unika personer. Den mäter inte ålder, funktionsförmåga eller digital vana. Telefonbokningarna kan därför inte användas för att säga hur stor andel av invånarna som inte kan boka digitalt.”

**Comparison:** “Too little” evaluates the totals against the decision and investigation the brief says Sanna advocates. It is not a numerical assessment that 24 bookings is high or low. The immediately following paragraph specifies the information limits. Supported as the author’s argument.

**Draft:** “The municipality’s pilot report, dated 8 April 2026, records 96 web bookings and 24 telephone bookings during an eight-week trial at two venues.”

**Source:** “Kommunens pilotrapport Bokning av föreningslokaler, 8 april 2026, gäller ett åtta veckor långt försök i två lokaler. Under försöket gjordes 96 bokningar via webb och 24 via telefon.”

**Comparison:** Municipality ownership, date, eight-week duration, two-premises scope, booking unit, channels and numbers match. The draft attributes both counts directly to the pilot report where they carry the argument, as the boundaries require. It does not turn counts into unique users, people or population shares. The document title is omitted without substituting a different named document. Supported.

### 12. Unit counted

**Draft:** “Those are bookings, not unique people.”

**Source:** “Rapporten räknar bokningar, inte unika personer.”

**Comparison:** “Those” refers to the 96 and 24 immediately preceding bookings. Both count and exclusion match. This does not state how many unique people booked. Supported.

### 13. Variables not measured

**Draft:** “The report measures neither age nor functional ability nor familiarity with digital technology.”

**Source:** “Den mäter inte ålder, funktionsförmåga eller digital vana.”

**Comparison:** The subject and all three excluded measurements match. In this user-access context, “functional ability” names the personal capacity denoted by “funktionsförmåga”, and “familiarity with digital technology” naturally denotes the practical digital familiarity denoted by “digital vana”. No particular diagnosis, disability prevalence or technical competence score is supplied. The wording does not mean merely knowledge of technology as an academic subject. No concrete contextual mismatch warrants a finding.

### 14. Telephone count and population inference

**Draft:** “So the telephone figure cannot tell us what proportion of Lervik’s residents cannot book online.”

**Source:** “Telefonbokningarna kan därför inte användas för att säga hur stor andel av invånarna som inte kan boka digitalt.”

**Comparison:** The antecedent is the reported count of 24 telephone bookings. Scope, population, channel and inability claim match. “Cannot tell us” preserves the source’s exclusion of that inference; it does not convert unknown inability into known ability. Supported.

### 15. Telephone use does not prove inability

**Draft:** “Nor does choosing the telephone prove an inability to use the web.”

**Source:** “Sanna Eks ståndpunkt: ‘Att en bokning går via telefon är inte ett bevis för att någon inte kan använda webben.’”

**Comparison:** This is an indirect rendering of Sanna’s explicitly supplied standpoint. Choosing telephone booking is not asserted to have any particular motive, and the sentence does not deny that an individual might be unable to use the web. “Choosing” fits the source’s later “varför de väljer telefon eller webb”; it does not assert unrestricted choice or the absence of barriers. ### 16. Reason to investigate

**Draft:** “It gives us a reason to ask why that route is still used.”

**Source:** “Det är ett skäl att ta reda på varför telefonen fortfarande används.”

**Comparison:** “It” is telephone booking/use, and “that route” is telephone booking. Ongoing use and the author’s reason to investigate match. No reason for using it is invented. Supported.

**Source:** “Under försöket ska förvaltningen registrera tidsåtgång per bokningsväg”

**Further source:** “Hon menar att kommunen först måste kunna väga arbetskostnaden mot värdet för användarna.”

**Comparison:** The proposed channel-specific timing and Sanna’s comparison underpin this evaluative subheading. “Fair” is her advocacy about how to assess the proposal, not an attributed finding that an existing measured comparison is unfair. Supported.

### 18. Administration’s objection and workflows

**Draft:** “The administration’s objection to keeping both routes is the administrative work across two channels: staff enter information in two workflows.”

**Source:** “Motivet i utlåtandet är att personalen ska slippa föra in uppgifter i två flöden. Någon tidsmätning eller ekonomisk besparingsberäkning finns inte i handlingarna. Förvaltningens verkliga invändning mot att behålla båda kanalerna är dubbel administration, inte att telefonanvändare är lata eller dyra.”

**Comparison:** The draft preserves the actual supplied objection and its stated operational basis. The source’s desire that staff be spared entering information in two workflows supports the work being avoided. It does not introduce an amount of time or money, laziness, expense per telephone user, party motives or a causal savings estimate. “Across two channels” is specified by the following clause; it does not reduce the objection to mere existence of two access routes. Supported.

### 19. Taking the concern seriously

**Draft:** “That concern deserves to be taken seriously.”

**Source:** “Förvaltningens verkliga invändning mot att behålla båda kanalerna är dubbel administration”

**Further source:** “Hon menar att kommunen först måste kunna väga arbetskostnaden mot värdet för användarna.”

**Comparison:** This is the author’s assessment of a supported objection. No outside party’s view is invented. It preserves the labour-cost side of the balance rather than changing the source’s factual motive. Supported argument.

### 20. Documentary absence, repeated in body

**Draft:** “But the documents provide no measurement of the time involved or calculation of financial savings.”

**Source:** “Någon tidsmätning eller ekonomisk besparingsberäkning finns inte i handlingarna.”

**Comparison:** The documentary scope and absent time/savings calculations match. The immediately preceding workflow detail settles “the time involved”. As in the standfirst, this is not a claim that nobody outside the documents has measured time or that savings are impossible. Supported.

### 21. Consequence for the board’s comparison

**Draft:** “Removing a route before establishing its value to users and the work it requires leaves the board without the comparison it needs.”

**Source:** “Hon menar att kommunen först måste kunna väga arbetskostnaden mot värdet för användarna.”

**Relevant factual source:** “Någon tidsmätning eller ekonomisk besparingsberäkning finns inte i handlingarna.”

**Proposed investigation:** “Under försöket ska förvaltningen registrera tidsåtgång per bokningsväg och be användarna frivilligt ange varför de väljer telefon eller webb.”

**Comparison:** This is Sanna’s argument for gathering the missing channel-specific evidence before a decision. It is conditional reasoning about removal before establishing the relevant comparison, not a report of an actual removal, a quantified causal effect, or an assertion that no information about users exists anywhere. “A route” is generic within the two-route proposal; “its” and “it” refer to that route. Supported argument.

### 22. Administrative simplicity and investigation

**Draft:** “Administrative simplicity is a reason to investigate the balance, not a substitute for doing so.”

**Source:** “Motivet i utlåtandet är att personalen ska slippa föra in uppgifter i två flöden.”

**Further source:** “Hon menar att kommunen först måste kunna väga arbetskostnaden mot värdet för användarna.”

**Comparison:** The first phrase characterises the supported aim of avoiding double administration. The rest is the author’s reasoning about what that aim justifies. No measured simplification, completed investigation or external consensus is claimed. Supported argument.

### 23. Third subheading: trial’s decision value

**Draft:** “A wider trial can inform the choice”

**Source:** “ett åtta veckor långt försök i två lokaler”

### 25. Data gathering and voluntary reasons

The draft’s “should” is a recommendation in the article and does not report an adopted administrative order. Voluntariness belongs to users giving reasons; the draft retains that scope. No age, disability or digital-literacy measurement is added. Supported.

### 26. Financing and costing: no claim

**Draft:** “We make no claim to have financed or costed that trial.”

**Source:** “Föreningen gör inget anspråk på att ha finansierat eller kostnadsberäknat försöket.”

**Comparison:** The preceding sentence identifies Öppna beslut, so “we” is the organisation speaking through its spokesperson. The draft retains the no-claim formulation. It does not replace it with an assertion that financing or costing definitely has not occurred. “Costed” is idiomatic British English for having calculated the trial’s costs. Supported.

### 27. Trial cost and board’s responsibility

**Draft:** “The executive board must consider its cost.”

**Source:** “Kostnaden behöver kommunstyrelsen ta ställning till.”

**Comparison:** The board and trial cost match. “Consider” alone is less explicit than taking a position, but the following sentence supplies the need to decide what the evidence-gathering is worth, and the final recommendation requires explicit cost consideration when agreeing the trial. Read in that context, the article does not claim a funded proposal or evade the board’s cost judgement. Supported; no factual certainty about the amount is introduced.

### 28. Evidence gathering also requires a decision

**Draft:** “Asking for better evidence does not remove the need to decide what gathering it is worth.”

**Source:** “Föreningen gör inget anspråk på att ha finansierat eller kostnadsberäknat försöket. Kostnaden behöver kommunstyrelsen ta ställning till.”

**Comparison:** This is the author’s reflection on the supported cost uncertainty and board responsibility. “It” refers to evidence, not an unidentified person. It adds no amount, available budget, financial calculation or claim of affordability. Supported argument.

### 29. Final subheading: evidence and decision

**Draft:** “Evidence should guide the final booking decision”

**Source:** “Tes: kommunstyrelsen bör skjuta upp ett permanent byte till enbart digital bokning av föreningslokaler och först pröva ett halvår med både telefon och webb.”

**Further source:** “Därefter kan den avgöra om en kanal ska tas bort, ändras eller behållas.”

**Comparison:** This is the commissioned evidence-first position. “Final” distinguishes the permanent channel decision from the preliminary trial; it does not claim the future decision is legally irrevocable. Supported advocacy.

**Draft:** “Lervik’s municipal executive board should now postpone the permanent switch and agree a six-month trial of both routes, with its cost explicitly considered.”

**Source:** “Tes: kommunstyrelsen bör skjuta upp ett permanent byte till enbart digital bokning av föreningslokaler och först pröva ett halvår med både telefon och webb.”

**Further source:** “Öppna beslut föreslår ett sex månader långt försök i alla sju lokaler, med båda bokningsvägarna kvar.”

**Cost qualification:** “Föreningen gör inget anspråk på att ha finansierat eller kostnadsberäknat försöket. Kostnaden behöver kommunstyrelsen ta ställning till.”

**Comparison:** The named body, requested postponement, permanent-change referent, six-month trial and two routes match. “Now” is the timing of the author’s recommendation, not an invented event date. “Agree” is part of that recommendation, not a reported approval. “Its cost explicitly considered” keeps the trial’s cost before the board; together with the preceding no-costing/no-financing-claim sentence it preserves the supplied uncertainty. Supported.

### 31. Final paragraph: available decisions after the trial

**Draft:** “After that, it can decide whether to remove, change or retain a booking channel.”

**Source:** “Kostnaden behöver kommunstyrelsen ta ställning till. Därefter kan den avgöra om en kanal ska tas bort, ändras eller behållas.”

**Comparison:** “It” denotes the named municipal executive board. The decision’s timing follows the proposed trial and cost consideration, as in the source’s trial-and-decision sequence. The modality “can” and all three possible channel outcomes match. The draft does not prescribe retention as the only acceptable final decision. Supported.

## Pronoun accounting

Person, number and natural gender are accounted for independently of merely locating each referent.

- **“I”** in “I do not oppose” and “I urge”: first-person singular, no natural gender encoded. The source supplies Sanna as the author/spokesperson, gives her non-opposition, and commissions the recommendation. Swedish “Hon” is third-person singular and naturally female; changing to the authorised first-person authorial voice adds no gender claim.
- **“Those”** in “Those are bookings”: plural demonstrative, no natural gender, referring to the reported bookings. Source “bokningar” and the two counts establish plurality.
- **“us”** in “tell us too little”, “cannot tell us” and “gives us a reason”: first-person plural, no natural gender. These are inclusive author-and-reader positions in an opinion article for residents. They do not identify a measured group or assert that every resident holds Sanna’s opinion. The factual inference limits remain those supplied.
- **“It”** in “It gives us a reason”: third-person singular, no natural gender, referring to the fact of telephone booking/use. Swedish “Det” similarly denotes that fact. Neither identifies a human whose gender would need support.

- **“That concern”** denotes double administration. Demonstrative singular, no natural gender; the source expressly supplies the objection.
- **“its”** in “its value to users” and **“it”** in “the work it requires”: third-person singular, no natural gender, referring to the hypothetical booking route. The source supplies routes and the cost/value comparison. The possessives do not assert a measured value or duration.
- **“it”** in “the comparison it needs”: third-person singular, no natural gender, referring to the board. The source assigns the decision and needed comparison to the municipality/board. It does not assert that the board has publicly adopted Sanna’s view.
- **“doing so”** refers to investigating the balance. It supplies no person, number or gender assertion.
- **“they”** in “why they choose”: third-person plural, natural gender unspecified, referring to users. Source “användarna” and “de väljer” establish plural users; no female or male user population is asserted.
